summary: Germany renews its attack toward Moscow in stages. The opening exposes conflicts between ambitious orders, depleted formations and the Soviet capacity to rebuild resistance.
body:
An offensive in instalments

On 15 November 1941, German infantry south of Kalinin advanced into positions the Red Army had left. Franz Halder, chief of the German Army General Staff, welcomed the withdrawal as a sign that Soviet resistance was weakening. Georg-Hans Reinhardt, commanding the neighbouring Third Panzer Group, saw something less encouraging. The defenders had placed screening troops forward, moved their main defence behind the Volga and destroyed the bridges the attackers had hoped to seize. The Germans had gained ground; the Soviet force had escaped another battle on unfavourable terms. The renewed offensive against Moscow began with disagreement about what an apparently successful advance meant.[1]

This was not the October offensive repeated with fewer kilometres left to travel. Operation Typhoon had opened with concentrated attacks and enormous encirclements. By mid-November, the German command was trying to recover decisive movement from an army whose remaining strength had already been consumed unevenly across a broad front. The new operation began in instalments: a corps of Ninth Army on the 15th, the northern panzer groups on the 16th, and Heinz Guderian's Second Panzer Army south of Tula on the 18th. Those intervals gave the fighting a different rhythm from the great opening blow of October. They also revealed how difficult it had become to assemble a simultaneous effort.[2]

The question was urgent because Army Group Centre had already spent much of the force with which it had begun Typhoon. Bock needed his northern and southern commands to converge while the Soviet high command rebuilt the defence between them. The opening days, followed here through the southern attack of 18 November and the reported Stalin–Zhukov exchange on the 19th, expose the assumptions behind that effort. German headquarters expected another concentrated exertion to break an opponent whose armies had repeatedly survived terrible defeats. Soviet headquarters had to keep those armies in action long enough for reinforcements to matter. Neither command could know the outcome from the first morning’s gains.[2][3]

The plan and its contradictions

Field Marshal Fedor von Bock's Army Group Centre stood in an arc west of Moscow. Adolf Strauss's Ninth Army held the northern sector extending toward Kalinin. Reinhardt's Third Panzer Group occupied the Lama River area west of Klin; Erich Hoepner's Fourth Panzer Group stood farther south, above the main Smolensk–Moscow highway. Günther von Kluge's Fourth Army covered the direct approaches and extended toward the Oka, where it connected with Guderian's Second Panzer Army. The Second Army protected the outer southern flank near Orel and Kursk. Each command had to maintain connections with its neighbours while moving along different roads against different Soviet formations.[2]

Bock's written objectives extended much farther than Moscow's immediate approaches. The Third and Fourth Panzer Groups were to cross the Moscow–Volga Canal and advance toward Rybinsk and Yaroslavl. In the south, Guderian was to reach Kashira; possibilities beyond it included turning toward Moscow or crossing the Oka toward Gorky. Kluge's Fourth Army would help close a nearer ring around the capital. These were several different operations embedded in one plan: a close envelopment, a deeper severing of communications, and an advance beyond the city. Each required infantry, bridging, transport and ammunition that would also be needed by the others.[2]

The contradiction was that Bock himself doubted whether his available tanks, men, and supplies could carry the northern forces beyond the canal or the southern forces beyond the Moscow River. He expressed those reservations while leaving the larger orders in force. His subordinates consequently had to reconcile ambitious written missions with increasingly restrictive practical guidance. Third Panzer Group later described the resulting uncertainty. A commander deciding whether to preserve a flank, pursue a retreating enemy, or push toward a distant crossing needed priorities that could survive contact with the actual condition of his troops. Bock's uncertainty made that calculation harder.[2]

The plan also made Kluge's performance crucial. His Fourth Army occupied the central sector that the armoured thrusts were supposed to envelop, but Soviet pressure near Serpukhov forced it to fight for its own position. On 18 November, Kluge would report some regiments reduced to four or five hundred men, with lieutenants commanding them, and consider a withdrawal toward the Protva. Bock wanted this army to help complete an encirclement; its commander was considering how to shorten a threatened front. The problem was present before any final dash to Moscow could begin. The southern armour could advance while the force meant to connect with it remained pinned down.[2]

What the staff already knew

The shortage of resources was not a discovery made after defeat. At the Orsha staff conference on 13 November, German officers discussed losses, vehicle availability, railway capacity, and the prospect of continued war in 1942. The figures preserved in the U.S. Army's documentary history are estimates reported within the German command: casualties of approximately 686,000 by 1 November, panzer divisions at roughly thirty-five percent of their original tank strength, and a motor fleet in which only about a third of vehicles were fully serviceable. Such aggregate figures cannot describe every battalion, but they show that the senior leadership knew the army had been profoundly diminished.[3]

German staff officers rated the army's 136 divisions in the east as the equivalent of eighty-three full-strength divisions. That was an assessment of effective strength, not a literal disappearance of fifty-three headquarters. The surviving formations still had to cover the fronts, guard the flanks and execute the missions assigned to their original establishment. Bock could concentrate his remaining mobile troops for another attack, but concentrating them did not restore the infantry elsewhere. The arithmetic helps explain why the army could appear formidable in a list of divisions while commanders at the front were already debating how much more ground their men could hold.[3][2]

The railway problem began with an incompatibility beneath the trains. Soviet broad-gauge track had to be converted before German rolling stock could run over it. Captured Soviet equipment offered only a partial alternative: the Orsha discussion counted about 500 locomotives and 21,000 wagons across the occupied eastern network, roughly a tenth of the stated requirement. These were theatre-wide estimates, not the rolling stock assigned to Bock alone. They nevertheless identified a difficulty common to every advancing army. Supplies could exist at a distant depot while the railway lacked the usable track or equipment to carry them forward. Winning another town did not resolve that shortage.[3]

Winter clothing that existed elsewhere

Winter clothing was among the supplies left in storage because moving it forward would displace other urgent consignments. The Orsha discussion thus recorded a failure of distribution as well as a shortage at the front. Ammunition, fuel, food and warm clothing were competing for the same transport capacity, although soldiers needed them together. A depot inventory could reassure a staff officer without warming a man on sentry duty. Continuing the offensive lengthened the final delivery journey and made that discrepancy harder to correct.[3]

Halder's argument for continuing was that the Soviet Union still possessed enough population and industry to restore its forces if allowed time. Stopping appeared to surrender the remaining chance to weaken that recovery. Yet attacking consumed precisely the men and machines Germany would need for the longer struggle Halder now anticipated. The conference reduced some projected objectives but retained the demand to extract further results before winter. This decision helps explain the offensive's persistence. Senior officers could recognise losses accurately and still draw an unsound conclusion about what those losses required them to do next.[3]

Halder’s conclusion left the army groups with different burdens. Army Group North was still expected to develop its Tikhvin operation and tighten the pressure on Leningrad. Army Group South was to continue, although the most distant objectives had been deferred. Army Group Centre was to increase pressure on Moscow without expecting substantial gains beyond it. The enormous design discussed before Orsha had contracted, but the troops were still to be driven for further results until about mid-December. There was no single remaining concentration capable of settling all three sectors. Each commander inherited a reduced objective alongside demands that his depleted formations would continue attacking.[3]

The armies facing the attack

Georgy Zhukov's Western Front defended the main approaches to Moscow, with Ivan Konev's Kalinin Front to its north and the Southwestern Front farther south. A Soviet front contained several armies, broadly comparable to a German army group. These boundaries became increasingly consequential as Bock's forces struck at the northern and southern ends of the defence. A reinforcement sent to Rokossovsky near Volokolamsk could not also strengthen Tula, while an attack near Kalinin required coordination with forces operating under a different front headquarters. Stalin's high command, the Stavka, had to decide which commanders would receive the reserves and when they could commit them.[2]

The defence was being reorganised as the attack approached. Zhukov had received the Fiftieth Army on 10 November when the Bryansk Front was dissolved; the Thirtieth Army would be transferred from Kalinin Front a week later. These changes brought the threatened northern and southern flanks under a more unified command, but command transfers did not automatically repair damaged communications or exhausted units. Konstantin Rokossovsky's Sixteenth Army and the neighbouring Thirtieth Army faced the developing northern threat. At Tula, the Fiftieth Army held a position whose survival constrained Guderian's freedom to move north.[2]

Replenishment during the pause had given Zhukov more than a change of orders. Soviet official figures, reproduced in the U.S. Army history, credited the Western Front with about 100,000 men, 300 tanks and 2,000 guns during the first half of November. These are aggregate reinforcement claims, not a count of equally trained soldiers and serviceable weapons assembled for one attack. They nevertheless indicate the scale of the effort to restore a defence after October's losses. The troops arrived into armies with different shortages and immediate dangers. Training, equipment, transport and the time available to integrate replacements all limited what the newly replenished formations could attempt.[2]

Stalin also demanded counterattacks. On 14 November, the Forty-Ninth Army struck Kluge's right flank near Serpukhov with cavalry, infantry and armour. Zhukov later recalled opposing such blows because he expected a German offensive shortly; his memoir explains his own position and deserves that attribution. The fighting itself is less ambiguous. Renewed Soviet attacks near Serpukhov obliged Kluge to retain forces and consider yielding ground just as Bock needed him to advance. A counterstroke that failed to destroy a German army could still disrupt its timetable and keep badly needed infantry away from a neighbouring thrust.[2]

The Soviet command also sought relief through operations outside the Moscow sector. The Kalinin and Southwestern fronts were to hold the outer flanks of Army Group Centre, limiting Bock's ability to transfer formations inward. Farther away, preparations at Rostov and Tikhvin aimed to force German commanders to attend to threats in their own sectors. Such operations could influence Moscow even when no unit moved directly from one battlefield to another: a reserve committed to restoring a threatened southern position could no longer be offered for a different purpose. The actual effects would depend on the attacks' success, but the intention was to make Germany sustain several urgent battles simultaneously.[2]

At Tikhvin, the difference between an instruction and a usable force was particularly stark. Meretskov had taken over the damaged Fourth Independent Army on 7 November. When he attacked on the 19th, the U.S. Army history records reinforcements of only one infantry division and two tank battalions. Those additions could affect a battle against an equally strained opponent, but they did not promise immediate relief for Moscow or Leningrad. The Stavka was trying to impose concurrent crises on the German commands with forces that were still being assembled. Its strategy depended on several difficult local battles becoming effective before any one threatened sector gave way.[2]

The memoir-based exchange between Stalin and Zhukov on 19 November conveys the waiting involved. As reproduced in the U.S. Army history, Stalin asked whether Moscow could be held; Zhukov requested two armies and two hundred tanks. Stalin promised the armies near the month’s end but said the tanks were unavailable. This is a later account of the conversation, not a surviving verbatim record inspected for this study. It nevertheless fits the documented sequence of reserve assembly. Zhukov had to hold with the forces already present while reinforcements existed partly as commitments and formations still on their way.[2]

Movement and resistance

The Ninth Army's advance on 15 November offered a narrow opening, not a general collapse. On the next day, the Third and Fourth Panzer Groups entered the offensive. The clash east of Volokolamsk was especially damaging to Soviet plans: a reinforced counterattack by Sixteenth Army's right flank met the German attack coming the other way. The Soviet force was driven back. The episode illustrates how intentions could collide before either side completed its preparations. An order to attack did not guarantee that a formation would choose the time, location, or circumstances of its first serious engagement.[2]

At the Lama, adjoining German formations experienced different openings. Stahel’s published chapter extract describes Seventh Panzer Division making slow progress on 16 November while Fourteenth Motorised Infantry Division obtained two bridgeheads. The mobile force did not simply sweep through a defence vacated the previous day. It still had to force crossings and bring supporting troops through them. This uneven progress mattered to the larger plan: neighbouring commands could begin their attacks within hours of each other and still emerge from the first day with very different prospects for continuing.[1]

Freezing ground initially helped the attackers by hardening surfaces that had trapped vehicles in autumn mud. German armour could again leave roads in places where the terrain permitted. Yet this improvement came with shorter days, snow, reduced visibility, and new mechanical and physiological burdens. Aircraft could not provide the same support whenever cloud or poor visibility intervened. Soldiers still had to dig, march, maintain weapons, and keep watch. Weather changed the balance of tasks; it did not supply the missing infantry or restore vehicles already worn out during the earlier campaign.[2]

Nor was Bock’s decision to persist merely imposed on a reluctant army by Hitler. On 18 November, Bock and Halder discussed the operation’s prospects and agreed that both sides were approaching exhaustion, making continued resolve decisive in their judgement. That interpretation turned German losses into an argument for another effort: if the opponent was equally depleted, stopping first might surrender victory. The defect lay in the comparison. German headquarters knew a great deal about their own depleted formations, but their estimate of Soviet remaining strength was much less secure. A sound account of German shortages could therefore coexist with an unsound decision about how to respond to them.[2]

The people inside the war

The defence of Moscow rested on work that operational summaries tend to compress into a phrase about reinforcements. Workers from the city and surrounding districts had been drawn into militia and rifle formations. Their civilian occupations did not disappear when they received military assignments: the population supplying defenders also had to keep transport, workshops, food distribution, and essential services functioning. The official military history records the formation of these units; its account also makes clear that experience and readiness varied. Mobilisation enlarged the pool of people available to the army while creating new burdens of training and support.[2]

Industrial evacuation also affected what the Soviet state could provide immediately. Mark Harrison describes factories moving to destinations where buildings, power and accommodation were unfinished. Preserving machinery was essential, but production stopped while it travelled and could remain interrupted after arrival. Workers and their families shared that displacement. The November defence depended on establishments still producing, stocks already accumulated and the uneven return to work of evacuated plants. The great later recovery of Soviet industry cannot be counted as equipment already available to Zhukov. At this stage, keeping an enterprise alive and obtaining another consignment of weapons from it were separate achievements.[4]

Captivity exposed Soviet soldiers to a different use of military resources. German authorities deprived prisoners of adequate food and shelter, subjected them to forced marches and shootings, and left them exposed to disease. These conditions were produced within a discriminatory system, not simply by the shortages experienced by German formations. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum documents prisoners digging holes for shelter and receiving less food than the already inadequate official provision. Winter intensified the mortality of people whom their captors had deliberately left unable to withstand it. Their fate belongs to the same campaign as the troops moving toward Moscow, even when operational accounts leave them behind the advancing front.[5]

A name recovered after seventy-one years

In his introduction to The Battle for Moscow, David Stahel describes a 2012 search near Vyazma that recovered a Soviet soldier whose identification paper remained legible. He gives the first name Sergei and records that a surviving sister was informed before a family reburial. This was a later recovery from the broader Moscow campaign, rather than an identified casualty of 15 November. Its value is precisely that limited, individual connection: a person missing from a family could be restored to it after decades in which military totals had offered no answer.[6]

Time in Moscow and Washington

On the same day that German infantry began moving south of Kalinin, an American memorandum recorded anxiety about a very different part of the struggle. W. Averell Harriman was concerned that a State Department communication on petroleum refining equipment and American technicians would make Soviet leaders doubt American sincerity. His secretary conveyed the concern to Edward Page, who recorded a dispute over consultation and responsibility now that aid was being handled through Lend-Lease. This was an internal American disagreement about how to fulfil a strategic commitment, not evidence that a particular cargo had reached the Soviet front.[7]

Harriman's concern connected a technical disagreement to a political danger. The Soviet leadership had accepted a promise of sustained American assistance, and delays or contradictory messages could make that promise appear unreliable. Yet Roosevelt's financing commitment of 30 October could not itself provide the ships, machinery, technicians and administrative agreement required to fulfil it. Washington was building a relationship whose larger material effects lay ahead. Moscow's immediate defence still depended on what could be brought into action during the next few days, while its survival would keep open the prospect of a much longer coalition war.[7][8]

The traffic in people ran westward as well. Rolf Keller’s study of Soviet prisoner labour records that by mid-November roughly 225,000 Soviet POWs were working in Germany, while many others were too weak for work. On 14 November, transports from the east were halted because of epidemic disease. The attempt to exploit prisoners collided with the debilitation that German policy had produced. Keller also describes reduced food allocations for men classified as unable to work, deepening the danger to precisely those who most needed recovery. These figures concern captivity in Germany, not prisoners employed around Moscow. They expose how military conquest, forced labour and discriminatory deprivation operated across the same war economy.[9]

By the opening week’s end, Bock could point to renewed movement but had no evidence that it would finish the war. The new attacks were drawing depleted German formations into fresh commitments while Soviet armies continued to receive men and equipment. At Tula, the next study’s focus, Guderian would attempt to bypass a city whose defenders remained in action. The southern advance would test whether the concentration ordered at headquarters could survive the separate demands of assault, flank protection and supply. The answer depended on the Red Army’s response as much as on the distance German vehicles could travel.[2]

sourceMethod: Numbered notes connect the prose to specific inspected passages. The U.S. Army campaign history is a retrospective synthesis, assessed alongside Soviet documentary transcriptions, institutional accounts and scholarship. Guderian’s and German signals officers’ postwar explanations are attributed; their criticisms of higher command are not independent proof of their own conduct. Public Cambridge extracts, edited diary selections and catalogue-only evidence are identified in the locators. Russian and German material is paraphrased in English; uninspected archival originals are not claimed as consulted. Orders, reported implementation and independently established outcomes remain distinct. Operational analysis is Ostkrieg’s interpretation of the cited evidence. This local editorial revision does not validate or update the companion maps or their cached passages.
